::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

:::



::: {.lesson-meta}
[Level 3 · Inference]{.level-3} [⏱ ~70 min]{} [Prerequisites: [Sampling distributions](../07-probability/30-sampling-distributions.qmd), [Bootstrap](../07-probability/31-bootstrap.qmd)]{}
:::

::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- build a confidence interval for a mean **by hand** and with `t.test()`;
- build a confidence interval for a proportion and explain why the simple "Wald" interval can fail;
- **simulate** the coverage of an interval and explain what the confidence level promises;
- predict how sample size and confidence level change the width of an interval;
- interpret a confidence interval correctly and spot the common wrong interpretations.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```
:::


## 1. Why a single number is not enough

The mean flipper length of the Adelie penguins in our data is about 190 mm. If a different team of researchers caught a different set of Adelie penguins, they would get a slightly different mean. In [Sampling distributions](../07-probability/30-sampling-distributions.qmd) we saw how much such estimates vary from sample to sample; in [Bootstrap](../07-probability/31-bootstrap.qmd) we estimated that variability by resampling.

A **point estimate** (one number) hides this uncertainty. A **confidence interval** (CI) reports a range instead:

> estimate ± margin of error

The margin of error is "a few standard errors": it tells the reader how far from the truth our estimate could plausibly be, given the size and noisiness of the sample.

## 2. A confidence interval for a mean, by hand

The recipe has three ingredients:

1. the **estimate**: the sample mean $\bar x$;
2. the **standard error** (SE): how much $\bar x$ typically varies between samples, $s / \sqrt{n}$;
3. a **multiplier** that sets the confidence level. For 95% and a mean, we use the 97.5% quantile of a t distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom (close to 2 for moderate $n$).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
adelie <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", !is.na(flipper_len)) |>
  pull(flipper_len)

n      <- length(adelie)
x_bar  <- mean(adelie)
se     <- sd(adelie) / sqrt(n)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)

c(lower = x_bar - t_crit * se, upper = x_bar + t_crit * se)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> lower upper 
#> 188.9 191.0
```


:::
:::


With $n =$ 151 birds the standard error is only 0.53 mm and the multiplier is 1.976, so the margin of error is 1.05 mm.

`t.test()` does the same calculation (and much more — see [t-tests](34-t-tests.qmd)). The interval is stored in `$conf.int`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ci_adelie <- t.test(adelie)$conf.int
ci_adelie
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 188.9 191.0
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- The two numbers are the **lower and upper limits**: 188.9 to 191 mm.
- `attr(,"conf.level")` reminds you of the confidence level used (0.95 by default; change it with `conf.level = 0.90`, for example).
- In words: *"Our best estimate of the mean flipper length of Adelie penguins is 190 mm; values between 188.9 and 191 mm are compatible with the data."*
:::

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: why the t distribution?

If the data come from a normal population, the standardised mean

$$
T = \frac{\bar X - \mu}{S / \sqrt{n}}
$$

follows a t distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. Therefore $P(-t_{0.975} \le T \le t_{0.975}) = 0.95$, and rearranging the inequality for $\mu$ gives the interval

$$
\bar x \pm t_{n-1,\,0.975}\,\frac{s}{\sqrt n}.
$$

We use $t$ rather than the normal quantile 1.96 because $s$ is itself an estimate: the extra uncertainty makes the tails heavier. The difference matters only for small samples: `qt(0.975, 4)` is 2.78, `qt(0.975, 29)` is 2.05, and `qnorm(0.975)` is 1.96. Thanks to the Central Limit Theorem the interval also works for non-normal data when $n$ is large enough — see Exercise 3 for a case where "large enough" matters.
:::

## 3. What "95%" really means: a simulation

Here is the most important idea of the lesson. The "95%" is **not** a property of one interval. It is a property of the **method**: if we repeated the whole study many times, building an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true value.

We can check this, because in a simulation *we* choose the truth. Let us invent a population with true mean $\mu = 50$ and standard deviation 10, draw 100 samples of size 20, and build 100 intervals.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
mu <- 50

cis <- replicate(100, t.test(rnorm(20, mean = mu, sd = 10))$conf.int)

sims <- tibble(
  id     = 1:100,
  lower  = cis[1, ],
  upper  = cis[2, ],
  covers = lower <= mu & mu <= upper
)
sum(sims$covers)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 96
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(sims, aes(y = id, colour = covers)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = id), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey60", `FALSE` = "#D55E00"),
                      labels = c(`TRUE` = "contains 50",
                                 `FALSE` = "misses 50")) +
  labs(x = "95% confidence interval", y = "Sample number", colour = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![100 confidence intervals from 100 samples of the same population. The dashed line is the true mean. Intervals that miss it are highlighted.](32-confidence-intervals_files/figure-html/fig-coverage-1.png){#fig-coverage fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


In this run, 96 of the 100 intervals contain the true mean and 4 miss it. Run it again with another seed and you will get a slightly different count, but close to 95. Notice two things in the figure:

- the intervals **move** (their centres are different sample means) and have **different widths** (each uses its own $s$);
- the true mean **does not move**. It is fixed; it is the intervals that are random.

With more repetitions the proportion settles very close to 0.95:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1)
covers <- replicate(5000, {
  ci <- t.test(rnorm(20, mean = mu, sd = 10))$conf.int
  ci[1] <= mu & mu <= ci[2]
})
mean(covers)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.9468
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## The correct interpretation

*"We used a method that captures the true mean in 95% of repeated samples. Applied to our sample, it gives the interval [a, b]."*

Once you have computed **your** interval, the true mean is either inside it or not — you just do not know which. The 95% describes how often the procedure works, not the probability for this one interval.
:::

## 4. What makes an interval wide or narrow?

The margin of error is multiplier × $s / \sqrt n$. So:

- **larger $n$** → smaller SE → narrower interval. Because of the square root, to halve the width you need about **four times** as many observations;
- **higher confidence level** → larger multiplier → wider interval. More confidence costs precision;
- **more variable data** (larger $s$) → wider interval.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
widths <- expand.grid(n = 5:100, level = c(0.90, 0.95, 0.99)) |>
  mutate(width = 2 * qt(1 - (1 - level) / 2, df = n - 1) / sqrt(n),
         level = factor(paste0(level * 100, "%")))

ggplot(widths, aes(n, width, colour = level)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Sample size n", y = "Interval width (in SD units)",
       colour = "Confidence level")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Expected width of a t-based interval (population SD = 1) as a function of sample size, for three confidence levels.](32-confidence-intervals_files/figure-html/fig-width-1.png){#fig-width fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


The same trade-off with real data:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sapply(c(0.90, 0.95, 0.99), \(lev) t.test(adelie, conf.level = lev)$conf.int)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>       [,1]  [,2]  [,3]
#> [1,] 189.1 188.9 188.6
#> [2,] 190.8 191.0 191.3
```


:::
:::


Each column is one interval (90%, 95%, 99%): they share the same centre and get wider as the level increases.

## 5. A confidence interval for a proportion

For a yes/no variable the estimate is the sample proportion $\hat p = x / n$ and its standard error is $\sqrt{\hat p (1 - \hat p) / n}$. The textbook ("**Wald**") interval is

$$
\hat p \pm 1.96 \sqrt{\hat p (1 - \hat p) / n}.
$$

Let us estimate the proportion of females among the penguins whose sex is recorded:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
n_known  <- sum(!is.na(penguins$sex))
x_female <- sum(penguins$sex == "female", na.rm = TRUE)
p_hat    <- x_female / n_known

wald <- p_hat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n_known)
wald
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.4418 0.5492
```


:::
:::


R offers two better intervals:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
prop.test(x_female, n_known)$conf.int    # Wilson score interval
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.4407 0.5504
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
binom.test(x_female, n_known)$conf.int   # Clopper-Pearson "exact" interval
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.4405 0.5505
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95
```


:::
:::


With 333 birds and $\hat p$ close to 0.5, the three intervals are practically identical. The trouble starts with **small samples or proportions near 0 or 1**. Suppose 2 of 20 patients have a side effect:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
p_small <- 2 / 20
p_small + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(p_small * (1 - p_small) / 20)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] -0.03148  0.23148
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
binom.test(2, 20)$conf.int
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.01235 0.31698
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95
```


:::
:::


The Wald interval has a **negative lower limit** — an impossible proportion. The interval from `binom.test()` stays inside [0, 1] and is asymmetric, as it should be when $\hat p$ is near the boundary.

The deeper problem is coverage. We can simulate it exactly as before: the true proportion is 0.10 and $n = 20$.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(3)
x_sim <- rbinom(5000, size = 20, prob = 0.10)

wald_covers <- sapply(x_sim, \(x) {
  p <- x / 20
  abs(p - 0.10) <= qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / 20)
})
exact_covers <- sapply(x_sim, \(x) {
  ci <- binom.test(x, 20)$conf.int
  ci[1] <= 0.10 & 0.10 <= ci[2]
})
c(wald = mean(wald_covers), exact = mean(exact_covers))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   wald  exact 
#> 0.8796 0.9884
```


:::
:::


The "95%" Wald interval actually captures the truth only about 88% of the time, while the exact interval covers at least 95% (it is deliberately conservative). **Recommendation:** use `prop.test()` or `binom.test()` and treat the Wald formula as a teaching device.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: Wilson and Clopper–Pearson

- **Wilson** (used by `prop.test()`, with a continuity correction by default) inverts the score test: it collects all values $p_0$ for which $|\hat p - p_0| / \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n} \le 1.96$. The SE is evaluated at $p_0$, not at $\hat p$, which keeps the interval inside [0, 1] and gives coverage close to 95% even for small $n$.
- **Clopper–Pearson** (used by `binom.test()`) inverts the exact binomial test. Its coverage is never below the nominal level, so it tends to be a little wide.
- The Wald interval fails because when $\hat p$ is near 0 or 1, $\sqrt{\hat p (1-\hat p)/n}$ underestimates the true SE (with $x = 0$ it is exactly 0: an interval of width zero!).

Proportions are tested formally in [Proportions and chi-square tests](35-proportions-chisq.qmd).
:::

## 6. A confidence interval for a difference in means

Very often the question is a comparison: *how much heavier are male Adelie penguins than females?* The same logic applies — estimate ± multiplier × SE — with the SE of a **difference**.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
adelie_sex <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", !is.na(sex))

ci_diff <- t.test(body_mass ~ sex, data = adelie_sex)$conf.int
ci_diff
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] -776.3 -573.0
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95
```


:::
:::


The interval refers to female − male (R orders the groups alphabetically): females are, on average, between 573 and 776 g lighter. The interval does not contain 0, so "no difference" is not a value compatible with the data. The full story — Welch's test, paired data, effect sizes — is in [t-tests](34-t-tests.qmd).

## 7. Right and wrong interpretations

Suppose a study reports a 95% CI for a mean of [12.1, 15.3].

| Statement | Correct? |
|---|---|
| "If we repeated the study many times, about 95% of the intervals computed this way would contain the true mean." | ✅ Yes — this is the definition. |
| "Values between 12.1 and 15.3 are compatible with the data; values far outside are not." | ✅ Yes — a useful practical reading. |
| "There is a 95% probability that the true mean is between 12.1 and 15.3." | ❌ No. The true mean is fixed; this particular interval either contains it or not. |
| "95% of the observations lie between 12.1 and 15.3." | ❌ No. The CI is about the **mean**, not individual values. Individual values are far more spread out. |
| "A second sample would give a mean between 12.1 and 15.3 with probability 95%." | ❌ No. The next sample mean has its own variability; this probability is noticeably lower than 95%. |
| "Two intervals that overlap mean the groups do not differ significantly." | ❌ Not necessarily. Two 95% CIs can overlap a little even when the difference is significant. Build a CI **for the difference** instead. |

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Reading a CI as a probability statement about the parameter.** The 95% is about the long-run behaviour of the method.
2. **Confusing the CI for a mean with the range of the data.** With large $n$ the CI becomes very narrow, while the data stay as spread out as ever.
3. **Using the Wald interval for small samples or extreme proportions.** It can leave [0, 1] and under-covers. Use `binom.test()` or `prop.test()`.
4. **Comparing groups by checking whether their separate CIs overlap.** Compute the interval of the difference.
5. **Forgetting what the interval cannot fix.** A CI accounts for *random sampling* error only. A biased sample (for example, only the penguins that were easy to catch) gives a precise interval around the wrong value.
:::

## 8. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. You quadruple the sample size. What happens, roughly, to the width of a 95% CI for a mean?

It is roughly **halved**, because the standard error is proportional to $1/\sqrt{n}$ and $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. A colleague computes a 99% CI and a 90% CI from the same data. Which one is wider, and why?

The **99%** interval. To capture the true value more often, the method must cast a wider net, so it uses a larger multiplier.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. In the simulation of Section 3, why did some intervals miss the true mean?

Because by chance those samples had a mean far from 50 (or an unusually small standard deviation). A 95% method is *expected* to miss in about 5% of samples — this is not a mistake in the code.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q4. In a survey, 0 of 15 people report a rare condition. What does the Wald interval give, and what should you use instead?

The Wald interval is $0 \pm 0$, i.e. [0, 0], which would claim we are certain the proportion is zero. `binom.test(0, 15)$conf.int` gives a sensible interval from 0 to about 0.22.
:::

## 9. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — CI for a mean.** Compute the 95% and the 90% confidence intervals for the mean `mpg` in `mtcars`. Which one is narrower?


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_32_1'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_32_1
ci95 <- t.test(mtcars$mpg)$______
ci90 <- t.test(mtcars$mpg, conf.level = ______)$conf.int
ci95
ci90
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_32_1"}
The interval is stored in the element `conf.int`; the level is a number between 0 and 1.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_32_1"}
```r
ci95 <- t.test(mtcars$mpg)$conf.int
ci90 <- t.test(mtcars$mpg, conf.level = 0.90)$conf.int
ci95   # about 17.9 to 22.3
ci90   # about 18.3 to 21.9
```
The 90% interval is narrower: lower confidence buys more precision.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — Wald versus exact.** In a small pilot study 3 of 15 participants dropped out. Compute the Wald 95% interval by hand and compare it with `binom.test()`. What is wrong with the Wald interval here?


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_32_2'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_32_2
x <- 3
n <- 15
p_hat <- x / n
se <- sqrt(______)
wald <- p_hat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
wald
binom.test(______, ______)$conf.int
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_32_2"}
The SE of a proportion is `sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)`. `binom.test()` takes the number of successes and the number of trials.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_32_2"}
```r
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
wald <- p_hat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
wald                         # about -0.002 to 0.40
binom.test(x, n)$conf.int    # about 0.04 to 0.48
```
The Wald interval dips below zero (an impossible proportion) and is symmetric even though $\hat p = 0.2$ is close to the boundary. The exact interval is asymmetric and stays within [0, 1].
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — does 95% always mean 95%?** Data from an exponential distribution (rate 1, true mean 1) are strongly skewed. Simulate 5,000 samples of size `n = 10`, build the t-based 95% interval each time and estimate its coverage. Then repeat with `n = 50`. What do you observe?


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_32_3'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_32_3
set.seed(1)
n <- 10
covers <- replicate(5000, {
  x  <- rexp(n, rate = 1)
  ci <- t.test(x)$conf.int
  ci[1] <= ______ & ______ <= ci[2]
})
mean(covers)
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_32_3"}
The true mean of `rexp(n, rate = 1)` is 1. Then change `n <- 10` to `n <- 50` and run again.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_32_3"}
```r
covers <- replicate(5000, {
  x  <- rexp(n, rate = 1)
  ci <- t.test(x)$conf.int
  ci[1] <= 1 & 1 <= ci[2]
})
mean(covers)   # about 0.90 with n = 10; about 0.93 with n = 50
```
With skewed data and a small sample, the "95%" interval covers the truth only about 90% of the time. With larger $n$ the Central Limit Theorem kicks in and coverage moves towards 95%. The confidence level is a promise that holds **only if the assumptions hold** (or $n$ is large enough). For skewed data, a bootstrap interval ([Bootstrap](../07-probability/31-bootstrap.qmd)) or a transformation can help.
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — one interval per group.** For each penguin species, compute the mean bill length (`bill_len`) and its 95% CI, and plot the three intervals with `geom_pointrange()`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
bill_ci <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(bill_len)) |>
  summarise(
    mean  = mean(bill_len),
    lower = t.test(bill_len)$conf.int[1],
    upper = t.test(bill_len)$conf.int[2],
    .by = species
  )
bill_ci

ggplot(bill_ci, aes(x = species, y = mean, ymin = lower, ymax = upper)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean bill length (mm) with 95% CI")
```
Adelie bills are clearly shorter (interval roughly 38.4 to 39.2 mm); the Chinstrap and Gentoo intervals (roughly 48.0–49.6 and 47.0–48.1 mm) are close to each other. To decide whether those two species differ, build an interval **for their difference** (Section 6), not by eye.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — interpret.** A news article says: *"The average commuting time is 32 minutes (95% CI 30 to 34). So 95% of commuters travel between 30 and 34 minutes."* Explain the error in two sentences and rewrite the second sentence correctly.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The interval is about the **average** commuting time, not about individual commuters: individual times vary far more (many people travel 10 or 60 minutes). A correct sentence is: *"Average commuting times between 30 and 34 minutes are compatible with the data; the method used captures the true average in 95% of repeated surveys."*
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it does |
|---|---|
| estimate ± multiplier × SE | General recipe for a confidence interval |
| `qt(0.975, df = n - 1)` | t multiplier for a 95% CI for a mean |
| `t.test(x)$conf.int` | CI for a mean (`conf.level =` to change the level) |
| `t.test(y ~ g, data = df)$conf.int` | CI for a difference in means |
| `prop.test(x, n)$conf.int` | Wilson CI for a proportion |
| `binom.test(x, n)$conf.int` | Exact (Clopper–Pearson) CI for a proportion |

- The confidence level describes the **method**: in repeated samples about 95% of intervals contain the truth.
- The parameter is fixed; the **interval is random**.
- Width shrinks with $\sqrt n$ and grows with the confidence level and with the variability of the data.
- For proportions, avoid the Wald interval with small $n$ or extreme $\hat p$.
- A CI covers sampling error only — not bias in how the data were collected.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
